is part of the Digital Analogues series, which examines the various types of persons or entities to which legal systems might analogize artificial intelligence (AI) systems. This post is the first of two that examines corporate personhood as a potential model for “AI personhood.” Future posts will examine how AI could also be analogized to pets, wild animals, employees, children, and prisoners.
Could the legal concept of “corporate personhood” serve as a model for how legal systems treat AI? Ever since the US Supreme Court’s Citizens United decision, corporate personhood has been a controversial topic in American political and legal discourse. Count me in the group that thinks that Citizens United was a horrible decision and that the law treats corporations a little too much like ‘real’ people. But I think the fundamental concept of corporate personhood is still sound. Moreover, the historical reasons that led to the creation of “corporate personhood”–namely, the desire to encourage ambitious investments and the new technologies that come with them–holds lessons for how we may eventually decide to treat AI.
An Overview of Corporate Personhood
For the uninitiated, here is a brief and oversimplified review of how and why corporations came to be treated like “persons” in the eyes of the law. During late antiquity and the Middle Ages, a company generally had no separate legal existence apart from its owner (or, in the case of partnerships, owners). Because a company was essentially an extension of its owners, owners were personally liable for companies’ debts and other liabilities. In the legal system, this meant that a plaintiff who successfully sued a company would be able to go after all of an owner’s personal assets.
This unlimited liability exposure meant that entrepreneurs were unlikely to invest in a company unless they could have a great deal of control over how that company would operate. That, in turn, meant that companies rarely had more than a handful of owners, which made it very difficult to raise enough money for capital-intensive ventures. When the rise of colonial empires and (especially) the Industrial Revolution created a need for larger companies capable of taking on more ambitious projects, the fact that companies had no separate legal existence and that their owners were subject to unlimited liability proved frustrating obstacles to economic growth.
The modern corporation was created to resolve these problems, primarily through two key features: legal personhood and limited liability. “Personhood” means that under the law, corporations are treated like artificial persons, with a legal existence separate from their owners (shareholders). Like natural persons (i.e., humans), corporations have the right to enter into contracts, own and dispose of assets, and file lawsuits–all in their own name. “Limited liability” means that the owners of a corporation only stand to lose the amount of money, or capital, that they have invested in the corporation. Plaintiffs cannot go after a corporate shareholder’s personal assets unless the shareholder engaged in unusual misconduct. Together, these features give a corporation a legal existence that is largely separate from its creators and owners.
The underlying theory of corporate personhood is based on economic and (supposedly) social utility. Corporations were granted contract and property rights to encourage investment and to facilitate large financial and property transactions, both of which were made easier by treating a corporation as an entity that is legally separate from its owner(s). Over time, corporations have accreted additional rights and responsibilities to promote other economic and social goals. The basic premise is that a corporation is a legal entity that the state treats like a “person” with respect to certain rights and responsibilities–and a person is, generally speaking, only responsible for his or her own conduct.
Would “AI Personhood” Be a Good Idea?
What lessons might corporate personhood hold for AI? Well, just as the traditional rules of business liability hindered the creation of sophisticated business entities, the traditional rules of products liability might hinder the creation of sophisticated AI systems. AI personhood, like corporate personhood, might prove an elegant solution to that potential problem.
Here’s why liability concerns might create a desire for AI personhood. As it stands, my anecdotal impressions from conversations with other lawyers is that courts would apply the ordinary rules of products liability to AI systems that cause harm. Those liability rules (at least in the United States) are in some ways reminiscent of the unlimited liability rules that traditionally applied to the owners of non-corporate companies. In most instances, a company is strictly liable for any harm caused by a defective product that it designed, manufactured, or sold. The “strict” part of strict liability means that the company can be held liable even if it was in no way negligent–just as a co-owner of a pre-corporate company could be liable even for debts and contracts that he played no role in creating.
Strict liability actually makes perfect sense and seems perfectly fair (to me, at least) for technologies whose mode of operation is mostly predictable. But with the advent of machine learning, how a learning AI system operates will be at least partially a function of its ‘experiences’ after it reaches a consumer–a period when the companies who designed, manufactured, and sold the AI system would no longer be able to control the system’s operation.
Because even the most careful designers and manufacturers will not be able to control or predict what an AI system will experience after it leaves their care, companies will have a strong incentive to limit the learning capabilities of AI systems, thus reducing the scope of AI systems’ ability to do things that it wouldn’t predict. That might sound like a good thing, just as keeping companies small and closely monitored by their owners sounds like a good thing in the business world. But the ability of AI systems to do things that their designers would not have predicted is actually part of what makes AI systems so enticing, as I argued in my recently published article:
Because A.I. systems are not inherently limited by the preconceived notions, rules of thumb, and conventional wisdom upon which most human decision-makers rely, A.I. systems have the capacity to come up with solutions that humans may not have considered, or that they considered and rejected in favor of more intuitively appealing options. It is precisely this ability to generate unique solutions that makes the use of A.I. attractive in an ever-increasing variety of fields.
Additionally, machine learning offers remarkable promise in terms of creating systems that can be tailored to the specific needs of each user in fields ranging from health care to consumer goods.
Consequently, to ensure that we can unlock the full potential of AI, we may eventually reach a point where it would make sense to recognize AI systems as having their own separate legal existence, with a corporation-like limitation of liability for the designers, manufacturers, and owners of AI systems.
What might AI personhood look like? What rights and responsibilities should AI systems have under the law? Under what circumstances might the designers, manufacturers, and owners of AI system be held liable for AI-caused harm if the AI system itself is a distinct person? Conferring limited personhood on artificial agents raises deep questions because international law has historically restricted legal personality to a narrow set of subjects: states as the primary and original bearers of rights and duties, individuals recognized especially after the human-rights movement following the Second World War, international organizations such as the United Nations, and multinational companies operating across borders [shard_02512_17215].
Three competing theories explain who qualifies as a subject of international law: the Realist theory that only states count, the Fictional theory that individuals are the true subjects behind every state duty, and the Functional theory that both states and individuals, plus entities like the African Union, can simultaneously hold recognized rights and obligations [shard_02512_17215].
This functional, criteria-based approach to personality is the strongest doctrinal opening for artificial agents, since it shows international law has already stretched personality beyond states without requiring human biology, but it also shows that each extension has been justified by a specific functional need, such as protecting human dignity or enabling treaty-making, a justification AI personhood has not yet clearly satisfied [shard_02512_17215].
A partial precedent for holding a non-state actor directly accountable is individual criminal responsibility under international law, established in Article 6 of the Nuremberg Charter, the 1948 Genocide Convention, and Articles 6 through 8 of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, which impose duties and liabilities on individuals irrespective of their state's domestic law [shard_04431_83489].
That regime nonetheless presumes a subject capable of intent, culpability, and punishment, qualities the "missing something" critique of AI personhood specifically denies, since AI systems are said to lack souls, consciousness, intentionality, feelings, and free will in the sense required for moral or criminal fault [shard_02299_4760].
Domestically, the clearest real-world attempt to translate this idea into policy was the European Parliament's 2017 proposal for "electronic personhood," which would have treated sophisticated learning robots as singular legal entities responsible for the damage they cause, backed by compulsory insurance funded from the wealth such robots accumulate [shard_00427_65708].
More than 150 experts across fourteen countries signed an open letter rejecting the proposal, arguing that a robot cannot be modeled on the Natural Person, since that would grant it dignity and citizenship rights conflicting with the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, nor on the Legal Entity model, since that model presumes real humans directing the entity, unlike a robot's autonomous operation, illustrated by their comparison that "your cat makes autonomous decisions too, but we do not hold the cat legally responsible" [shard_00427_65708].
The European Commission ultimately declined to adopt electronic personhood, reflecting the view that the concept was premature relative to actual machine capability [shard_03088_54559].
Traditional corporate personhood offers the closest analogy and the sharpest contrast to AI personhood, because corporations were granted legal personality and limited liability specifically to solve the historical problem of unlimited personal liability discouraging large capital-intensive investment during the Industrial Revolution, a problem with a clear economic justification and clear human principals standing behind the entity [shard_04517_13603].
The foundational case Salomon v. Salomon & Co. established that a company has an independent legal existence separate from its members, a doctrine later imported into jurisdictions including India, while still denying the corporation attributes reserved for natural persons, such as citizenship [shard_03088_54559].
Corporate personhood's liability shield is not absolute: courts can pierce the corporate veil under alter-ego or instrumentality theories when shareholders blur the line between themselves and the entity, restoring personal liability to reach an equitable result, a check that has no clear machine-learning equivalent because an AI system cannot be shown to be someone's "alter ego" in the same evidentiary sense [shard_06431_29444].
The critical disanalogy is that corporate personhood always retains identifiable human principals, directors, and shareholders behind the veil, whereas granting an AI system personhood risks creating a liability sink with no natural person ultimately answerable, which is precisely why critics warn it would let manufacturers "off the liability hook" [shard_00427_65708].
The UAE illustrates a materially different governance model that regulates AI without conferring it personhood at all, instead building an institutional and ethical scaffolding around human ministries and councils.
The UAE launched its 2017 Strategy of Artificial Intelligence, created the ministerial post held by Omar bin Sultan al-Olama, and established the UAE Council for Artificial Intelligence in 2018, later superseded by the ten-year National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2031 aimed at embedding AI across government sectors [shard_05653_68767].
The AI governance council is chaired by the Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications, and it operates through the UAE's own AI Ethics Principles of transparency, accountability, and fairness, alongside Digital Dubai's Ethical AI Toolkit, deliberately keeping accountability anchored in human institutions rather than shifting it to the machine [shard_00845_7520].
Minister al-Olama himself has framed this approach as prioritizing tangible impact on people over "fancy or gimmicky" AI applications, and Dubai's 2019 "AI Ethics, Principles and Guidelines" signaled an intent to move toward a mandatory legislative framework while weighing concerns that overly rigid law could stifle innovation [shard_03363_22552].
This is the core structural difference from electronic personhood: the UAE model layers ethical principles and ministerial oversight onto existing human and corporate legal persons, so liability logically continues to trace back to developers, operators, or the state, whereas personhood proposals attempt to interpose a new legal subject between the harm and those human actors [shard_00845_7520] [shard_00427_65708].
Turning to liability and accountability challenges more specifically, no single existing legal theory maps cleanly onto autonomous AI, and at least eleven adapted models have been proposed, including data-protection law, contractual liability, negligence, vicarious liability analogized to an employer-employee or corporate-manslaughter relationship, statutory insurance modeled on the UK's Automated and Electric Vehicles Act, strict animal-liability analogies, products liability, abnormally-dangerous-goods liability, and criminal-law constructs such as "perpetrator-via-another" and "natural-probable-consequence," each carrying its own defects [shard_01093_73320].
Negligence claims struggle because a defendant needs an identifiable duty of care, yet it is unclear whether that duty attaches to the developer, manufacturer, operator, or insurer, and criminal liability struggles because actus reus is easy to assign to an AI's output while mens rea, or culpable mental intent, has no clear locus in a machine [shard_01093_73320].
The "black box" opacity of modern machine-learning systems compounds this, since decisions often cannot be traced back to the specific data or code that produced them, undermining both tort causation analysis and insurers' existing risk models built for predictable products [shard_01093_73320].
A further proposed solution allocates strict liability to manufacturers, who hold the most knowledge and control over risk and thus the greatest incentive to mitigate it, but this risks discouraging investment and innovation, especially since manufacturers cannot fully control how operators deploy a system after release [shard_03541_72340].
Because responsibility is genuinely multi-causal, spread across programmers, data providers, manufacturers, third parties who manipulate the system, and operators, some scholars propose "propositional" or shared liability, or pooling risk through community insurance akin to social-security schemes, to avoid the complexity of assigning fault to one party while still discouraging negligence [shard_03541_72340].
Granting AI limited personhood is sometimes proposed precisely to resolve these liability puzzles, by making the AI system itself absorb legal responsibility while its own accumulated assets and mandatory insurance satisfy injured parties, mirroring how corporate personhood once solved unlimited investor liability [shard_04517_13603] [shard_00427_65708].
Yet this "solution" imports the corporate model's central vulnerability without its central safeguard, since a corporation's veil can be pierced back to responsible humans while an AI's operations may leave no comparably clear evidentiary path back to a culpable designer or user, meaning personhood could simply relocate liability into an under-capitalized legal shell rather than resolve accountability at all [shard_00427_65708] [shard_06431_29444].
Taken together, the evidence suggests international law's flexible, functionally justified conception of legal personality could theoretically accommodate a narrow, purpose-specific form of AI personhood, but only if paired with mechanisms, comparable to piercing the corporate veil, mandatory insurance, or joint liability, that keep a traceable line back to accountable humans, a pairing current proposals like the EU's rejected electronic-personhood scheme and the UAE's human-centered ministerial model have approached in opposite ways: one by creating a new legal subject, the other by strengthening oversight of existing subjects [shard_00427_65708] [shard_00845_7520] [shard_02512_17215].
